sources.cite: Schulz-Menger J, Collini V, et al. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J 2025;46(40):3952-4041. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
sources.note: Section 11.8: tamponade is a pericardial syndrome in which an effusion impairs diastolic filling until cardiac output falls; blood in the pericardium can cause it at 200-300 mL; after trauma or cardiac surgery an effusion may be loculated and press on one chamber. 11.8.2: a clinical diagnosis, confirmed by echo. 11.8.3: drainage (needle pericardiocentesis preferred; surgical drainage preferred for bleeding into the pericardium); avoid diuretics and positive-pressure ventilation; temporary fluid can stabilise the patient while drainage is arranged. This case offers no diuretic and re-explores for bleeding, so no action here is a guideline-named contraindication; the patient is already ventilated, which the case does not change. Protamine with a normal ACT and dobutamine in tamponade are scored as poor choices and listed for clinical review (docs/sims.md 3.2). Section numbers and wording come from the coordinator's reading of the publisher's free-access page, relayed to the author of this entry, who could not open the full text; confirm them against the guideline at the next review.

sources.cite: Adler Y, Charron P, et al. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases. Eur Heart J 2015;36(42):2921-2964
sources.note: Kept only for the one point the 2025 guideline (as relayed) does not cover: vasodilators in tamponade are not recommended (class III, level C). This case offers none before re-exploration (nicardipine appears only in phase 2, after the tamponade is relieved). Its diuretics recommendation is now covered by the 2025 guideline above, which supersedes this one for everything else.

brief.situation: Handover at 14:00. Bed 6, 64-year-old, CABG x3 (LIMA-LAD, SVG-OM, SVG-RCA) finished at 10:00. Sedated and on the ventilator, FiO2 0.40. Two mediastinal chest tubes to -20 cmH2O suction. Pulmonary artery catheter. Epicardial pacing wires with the pacer box at the bedside, off (sinus rhythm).
handover: Chest tube drainage 80-120 mL/h for the last 3 hours, dark red.
HR 88, ABP 118/70, CVP 8, PAOP 12 mmHg, CI 2.6 L/min/m2, SvO2 68%.
Post-op Hgb 9.6 g/dL. ACT back to baseline after protamine in the OR. No vasoactive drips running.
howItWorks: The clock runs in real time: one minute on the monitor is one minute for you. Pause any time.
Assessments examine the patient; orders act. Some ask for a dose or volume.
Everything takes as long as it would on a real unit: a bolus runs in over minutes, drips take minutes to work, the surgeon calls back and walks over, labs and echo take time.
While you wait on something, Skip jumps ahead, says how much time it skips and logs it. The patient keeps changing at the same rate.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. Then a debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Sedated on the ventilator. Warm and pink, cap refill under 2 s.
Paler than before. Hands cooling, cap refill 3 s. Neck veins look fuller.
Pale and clammy, mottled knees, cap refill over 4 s. Distended neck veins with the head of bed at 30 degrees. The arterial trace swings with each ventilator breath.
S1 and S2 clearly heard. No rub, no new murmur.
Heart sounds are quieter than at handover.
Heart sounds muffled and distant.
Dark red drainage, steady. Fluctuation (tidaling) in the water seal. No clots seen.
Draining again in small amounts since the clots were cleared.
Drainage has slowed to almost nothing again. No tidaling.
Drainage has stopped. Dark clot in the tubing near the chest wall. No tidaling.
Tubes patent, tidaling in the water seal, no clots. Drainage steady.
Clots in the mediastinal tubing. Clearing them per protocol over the next couple of minutes: 120 mL dark blood and clot out. Drainage resumes, but more clot is likely still around the heart.
Small clots again, 20 mL out. Little drainage. The problem is inside the chest, not in the tubing.
PAOP {paop} mmHg with CVP {cvp}. Right and left filling pressures are nearly equal.
PAOP {paop} mmHg with CVP {cvp}. The gap between CVP and PAOP is narrowing.
PAOP {paop} mmHg with CVP {cvp}.

then.log: Cardiac index rises to 2.5, PAOP falls to 15 and SvO2 recovers to 66%. Feet warming, cap refill 2 s, urine picking up. Lactate trending down.
Filling pressures climb (PAOP 24) but cardiac index barely moves. SpO2 drifts to 93% with new crackles at the bases. The ventricle is already full; it needs help squeezing.
MAP looks better (84) but cardiac index falls to 1.6 and SvO2 to 50%. More afterload on a stunned ventricle: pressure up, flow down. Lactate rising.
Cardiac index nudges to 2.0 but MAP drops to 60. Afterload reduction can help a failing ventricle, but not on its own when pressure is already marginal.

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Names cardiac tamponade (clot around the heart after surgery) and supports it with at least two of: drainage that suddenly stopped, hypotension with tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, CVP and PAOP rising together, muffled heart sounds, falling CI or SvO2.
parts.modelAnswer: Cardiac tamponade from clot in the mediastinum: drainage suddenly stopped after steady output, hypotension with tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, CVP and PAOP rising toward each other, falling CI and SvO2, quieter heart sounds. Hypovolemia does not raise filling pressures.

parts.label: What first
parts.criteria: Calls the cardiac surgeon to the bedside now (surgical re-exploration is the fix); treats fluid and drips as a bridge only; mentions echo, resternotomy preparation or OR notification.
parts.modelAnswer: Call the cardiac surgeon and ask them to come now, because re-exploration is the fix. Bridge with a small bolus and a low-dose vasopressor, get a STAT echo, prepare for resternotomy and notify the OR, draw labs.

early.label: Stable: early re-exploration

early.narrative: Early re-exploration and the low-output state treated with an inotrope. Recognition and escalation were early, so the patient never got close to arresting.

earlyUntreated.label: Early re-exploration, low output not fully treated
earlyUntreated.narrative: The surgeon came early and the tamponade was fixed, but either re-exploration started later than 45 minutes after the drainage stopped or the stunned ventricle after surgery did not end up on an inotrope.

bridge.label: Stable, by a slower route
bridge.narrative: The patient made it to re-exploration and is stable, but with more clot, more blood and more support than an earlier call would have needed.

late.label: Late rescue: emergency bedside resternotomy
late.narrative: The patient survived, but only through an emergency reopening at the bedside. A late rescue: higher risk of infection, kidney and brain injury.

arrestRosc.label: Survived a cardiac arrest
arrestRosc.narrative: The patient arrested from tamponade and came back after the chest was reopened at the bedside. Survival after a rescue: higher risk of brain, kidney and infection complications than an early return to the OR.

expertPath.text: Notice drainage falling from about 100 mL/h to almost nothing (at the latest by the 14:15 q15-min check). Inspect the tubes, clear them per protocol (clots found).
Put it together: rising HR, narrowing pulse pressure, CVP rising toward PAOP, quieter heart sounds. Suspect tamponade.
Page the cardiac surgeon and give an SBAR asking them to come now. Callback about 2 min, at the bedside about 10 min later.
STAT bedside echo (about 10 min), resternotomy tray to the bedside, OR and perfusion notified, labs drawn (blood gas and ACT back in about 5 min, coags about 45 min).
Bridge only: 250 mL bolus (about 5 min to run in), low-dose norepinephrine titrated every 5 min to hold MAP at 65 or more while the surgeon comes.
Surgeon at the bedside; echo confirms. OR already prepared, so the patient is in the OR about 15 min later (about 40 min after the drainage stopped).
Low CI with high PAOP and cool extremities after re-exploration: add an inotrope, hold MAP with norepinephrine, no more fluid. Reassess at about 30 min.

early.headline: Stable: early re-exploration
early.body: You spotted the change and got the surgeon there early. That is the expert path.

earlyUntreated.headline: Early re-exploration, then a gap
earlyUntreated.body: The surgeon came early. The minutes after the operation are where to look: re-exploration later than 45 minutes after the drainage stopped, or a stunned ventricle left without an inotrope.

bridge.headline: Stable, by a slower route
bridge.body: Re-exploration came after the clot had grown: more blood and more support than an earlier return would have needed. Paging the surgeon to the bedside within about 20 minutes of the drainage stopping, with the OR already notified, is what turns this into the expert path.

late.headline: Late rescue: emergency bedside resternotomy
late.body: The patient survived, but only through an emergency reopening at the bedside. The minutes before the call are where to look.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: The run reached its time limit.

arrestRosc.headline: Back from an arrest
arrestRosc.body: The arrest was survivable because the cause was mechanical and the chest was reopened fast. Look at when the clot could have been caught: the drainage that stopped, the narrowing pulse pressure, the rising CVP.

scoring.modelReasoning: Cardiac tamponade from clot in the mediastinum. The clues: chest tube drainage that suddenly stopped after hours of steady output, hypotension with tachycardia, a narrowing pulse pressure, CVP and PAOP rising and moving toward the same number (equalisation), falling cardiac index and SvO2, muffled heart sounds and falling urine output. Hypovolemia does not raise filling pressures. Priority: call the cardiac surgeon now and ask them to come to the bedside, because the fix is surgical re-exploration, and getting the surgeon there takes minutes you cannot get back. While waiting: support the pressure (small fluid bolus, vasopressor as a bridge), get a STAT echo, prepare for emergency resternotomy and notify the OR, and draw labs. Fluids and drips buy minutes, not a cure.

etiology.arrestLog: PEA: organised rhythm on the ECG, no pulse on the arterial line. The clot has stopped the heart from filling. Cardiac arrest after cardiac surgery: call the arrest and start the protocol.

source.note: Tick 780 is 11 min after onset (the drainage stops at 120 s), inside the brief's 10 to 12 min. With no learner action the first reasoning moment opens at tick 840 and no alarm has fired by 780, so the start is reached by evolving the normal start with no actions and leaves the first clear deterioration to the learner.

cvpAfterBolus.ask: What do you expect the CVP to do as this bolus goes in?

choices.label: Rise
Stay about the same
Fall

cvpAfterBolus.explain: It rises. In 49 patients with tamponade, a 500 mL saline bolus raised the right atrial pressure by about 3 mmHg on average. Cardiac output rose in about half of them, stayed the same in about a fifth and fell in about a third, and a low systolic pressure (under 100) predicted who benefited. So fluid can buy a little time, it is not the fix. The 2025 European guideline also says temporary fluid can stabilise a patient while drainage is arranged, which fits.

source.cite: Sagrista-Sauleda J, et al. Hemodynamic effects of volume expansion in patients with cardiac tamponade. Circulation 2008;117:1545-1549
source.note: Right atrial pressure 9.8 to 12.8 mmHg; cardiac index up by more than 10% in 47%, unchanged in 22%, down in 31%; baseline systolic under 100 mmHg predicted a response. FLAG: the patients had large pericardial effusions from medical causes, not early post-cardiac-surgery bleeding, and the bolus was 500 mL over 10 min; it is used here for the direction of the CVP and the unreliable benefit only. The 2025 ESC guideline (Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952, section 11.8.3, as relayed) agrees that temporary fluid can stabilise the patient while drainage is arranged; it gives no CVP figure, so the direction of the CVP rests on Sagrista-Sauleda alone.

echoNormal.ask: The echo is being done. If it looks normal, what does that tell you this soon after surgery?

choices.label: Tamponade is ruled out
Not ruled out: an early echo can miss it
Ruled out only if the pictures are clear

echoNormal.explain: Not ruled out. The 2025 European guideline calls tamponade a clinical diagnosis that echo confirms, and notes that after cardiac surgery a collection may be loculated, pressing on just one part of the heart. Separately, one study of 427 echoes within 4 weeks of cardiac surgery found echo accuracy poor in the first 24 hours, and in another 13 of 22 tamponades missed by a standard chest echo were found by an echo through the esophagus. The picture at the bedside still decides.

source.cite: Schulz-Menger J, Collini V, et al. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J 2025;46(40):3952-4041. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
source.note: ESC 2025 section 11.8 (as relayed) supports two things only: tamponade is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo (11.8.2), and after trauma or cardiac surgery an effusion may be loculated and cause localised compression (11.8). It does NOT say whether a normal transthoracic echo excludes tamponade and does not cover transesophageal echo. Those two statements rest on separate sources: (1) Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2022;62:ezab468, doi 10.1093/ejcts/ezab468, 427 echocardiograms within 4 weeks of cardiac surgery, 105 of 116 re-explorations found tamponade, accuracy acceptable overall but poor in the first 24 h; (2) J Card Surg 2008;23:450-453, doi 10.1111/j.1540-8191.2008.00581.x, 13 of 22 tamponades missed by transthoracic echo were found by transesophageal echo and confirmed at surgery. FLAG: both are retrospective single-centre data, and the first paper's score for the early phase is in the full text, which the author of this prompt could not read. Section numbers and wording come from the coordinator's reading of the publisher's free-access page, relayed to the author of this entry, who could not open the full text; confirm them against the guideline at the next review.

triad.ask: While you wait for the call back: the classic triad (low pressure, raised venous pressure, quiet heart sounds) is seen in surgical tamponade. Wait for all 3?

choices.label: Yes, wait until all three show
No: act on the pattern you already have

triad.explain: No. The 2025 European guideline says the triad (low blood pressure, raised jugular venous pressure, quiet heart sounds) is classically seen in surgical tamponade and may be absent in medical tamponade, so you might see it here. But it is the classic picture, not a requirement, and the guideline describes tamponade as a clinical diagnosis. A review of tamponade also notes that the full triad is uncommon in practice. Act on the pattern you already have: a falling drainage, a rising heart rate, a narrowing pulse pressure and a CVP rising toward the wedge.

source.cite: Schulz-Menger J, Collini V, et al. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J 2025;46(40):3952-4041. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
source.note: ESC 2025 section 11.8.1 (as relayed): Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds) is classically seen in surgical tamponade and may be absent in medical tamponade; the guideline also lists pulsus paradoxus (an inspiratory systolic drop of 10 mmHg or more), low QRS voltage and electrical alternans; 11.8.2: a clinical diagnosis. Changed from the first version, which asked whether the triad would show and answered 'probably not' on Alerhand S, et al. Am J Emerg Med 2022;58:159-174 (doi 10.1016/j.ajem.2022.05.001) alone: for surgical tamponade the guideline puts it the other way round, so the prompt now asks whether to wait for it. 'Uncommon in practice' is that review's statement about tamponade in general. FLAG: the last sentence of the explanation restates this scenario's own expert path, not a finding of either source. Section numbers and wording come from the coordinator's reading of the publisher's free-access page, relayed to the author of this entry, who could not open the full text; confirm them against the guideline at the next review.

echoSigns.ask: While the surgeon walks over: which of these echo findings is the least specific for tamponade, so it cannot confirm it on its own?

choices.label: The right ventricle collapses in diastole
A wide vena cava that does not collapse when the patient breathes in
The right atrium stays collapsed for more than a third of the heartbeat

echoSigns.explain: The wide vena cava that does not collapse. In the 2025 European guideline's summary of echo signs it is the most sensitive of these (about 97%) but the least specific (about 40%): it is also seen in many people who do not have tamponade. Right ventricular collapse in diastole (specificity about 72 to 100%) and right atrial collapse lasting more than about a third of the cycle (specificity reported as 100%) are far more specific. The echo supports the clinical picture; it does not replace it.

source.cite: Schulz-Menger J, Collini V, et al. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J 2025;46(40):3952-4041. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
source.note: ESC 2025 section 11.8.2, Table 17 (as relayed): RA diastolic collapse sensitivity 50-100%, specificity 33-100%; RA collapse longer than 0.34 of the cycle sensitivity above 90%, specificity 100%; RV diastolic collapse sensitivity 48-100%, specificity 72-100%; respiratory variation of mitral E above 25-30% or tricuspid E above 40-60%; IVC plethora sensitivity 97%, specificity 40%. Changed from the first version, which asked which sign is 'most specific' and answered right ventricular collapse on Alerhand 2022: Table 17's ranges overlap (RV 72-100%, RA over a third of the cycle 100%), so no single 'most specific' sign is supported, but the least specific of these three is. Plain RA collapse (specificity 33-100%) is left out of the options for that reason. FLAG: the ranges come from small studies, mostly of medical effusions, and the figures are relayed, not read from the table by this author. Section numbers and wording come from the coordinator's reading of the publisher's free-access page, relayed to the author of this entry, who could not open the full text; confirm them against the guideline at the next review.
